claim_reviews.analysis: Mechanism is confirmed verbatim in source. rewrite_lvalue (687-698) takes bound but applies it only to the Index sub-expression (692, via rewrite_expr); the LValue::Var name and the LValue::Index name both go through rewrite_state_name (700-706), which qualifies a name iff component.names.state.contains(&name) and never inspects bound. This is asymmetric with rewrite_statement's ForAll arm (675-680), which clones bound and inserts the binder before rewriting the body, and with rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717), which guards on !bound.contains(&name). So once a binder name is inserted into bound for a body, an assignment/index target to that name is still prefixed to alias.x while the identical name in the rvalue is left bare — the exact alias.x := f(x) split the claim describes. The path is reachable: rewrite_statement Assign (655) passes the threaded bound to rewrite_lvalue, and the ForAll arm supplies a non-empty nested bound. The inconsistency is a real defect independent of the trigger. Two parts are inferential, not shown by projections: that the surface grammar actually permits a binder to shadow a component state name (if shadowing is illegal the defect is latent), and the 'corrupts the kernel' consequence (no runtime/kernel behavior in any projection).
unsupported_assumptions: the surface language permits a binder to shadow a component state name (legality of shadowing is not in any received projection); if forbidden, the trigger is unreachable and the defect is latent
the downstream 'silently corrupts the kernel' consequence is inferred — no kernel/runtime behavior or downstream consumer is in the projections
that the observed asymmetry (lvalue ignores bound, rvalue honors it) is an unintended omission rather than an intentional scoping rule for lvalues

claim_reviews.analysis: Confirmed by source. rewrite_action_items (609-631) is a single .map(|item| ...) over the iterator, so every item is transformed against the same immutable bound with no threading of state between items; the Let arm (623-625) rewrites only the initializer via rewrite_expr and never inserts name into bound. Consequently a subsequent item's rvalue reference to that name is rewritten by rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717), where !bound.contains(&name) still holds, so if name is in component.names.state or component.names.consts it is prefixed to alias.name — i.e. resolved to the state/const rather than the local let. This contrasts with the bound-extending pattern the claim cites and which is present in source: Expr::Quantified (796-802) and Expr::Aggregate (810-816) both clone bound, insert the binder, then rewrite the body with &nested, and rewrite_binder (844-855) likewise clones bound and inserts the name (854-855). The Let arm is the only action-level binder that does not extend bound, and the .map structure makes extension impossible without a rewrite of the function. Let is handled only here (it is an ActionItem, not a Statement), so there is no other path that would add its name to bound. The defect is structurally real. Inferential parts: that a let name may shadow a state/const name (legality not in projections), and that the later reference is an Expr::Var carrying the bare name (a reasonable but assumed reading of 'referencing n in an rvalue').
unsupported_assumptions: the surface language permits a let-bound name to shadow a component state or const name (legality not established by projections)
the later referencing item encodes the name as Expr::Var in an rvalue position (assumed, not shown)
that the correct semantics is local-shadow-wins (so the local let should suppress qualification), which is an interpretation of intent rather than a projected fact

finding.description: rewrite_lvalue (compose.rs:687-698) rewrites LValue::Var and LValue::Index names via rewrite_state_name (700-706), which prefixes any name in component.names.state without consulting bound; bound is used only for the Index sub-expression, never for the variable name itself. This contradicts the design: rewrite_statement's ForAll arm (670-683) deliberately extends bound with the binder before rewriting the body, and rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717) honors bound. Trigger: a ForAll/Quantified/Aggregate whose binder shadows a component state name, with an assignment or index to that name in the body (e.g. `ForAll (x: T) { x := f(x) }` when the component also declares state `x`) lowers to a write on the component's qualified state `x` instead of the binder, silently corrupting the kernel.
finding.title: Lvalue rewrite ignores the bound set, so a binder shadowing a state name corrupts assignment targets

finding.description: rewrite_action_items (609-631) rewrites each ActionItem independently with the same bound reference; the Let arm (623-625) never inserts the newly bound name into bound, unlike rewrite_binder (844-855), Expr::Quantified (796-798) and Expr::Aggregate (810-812), which all clone bound and insert the binder before rewriting the body. Trigger: an action containing `let n = ...` where `n` matches a component state or const name, followed by any later item referencing `n` in an rvalue — rewrite_expr (711-717) then rewrites `n` to `alias.n` (the state/const) instead of the local binding, since `!bound.contains(&n)` still holds.
finding.title: Let bindings in rewrite_action_items do not extend bound, so later uses of a let name that shadows a state/const are mis-qualified

finding.description: rewrite_expr ends in `other => other` (840) and rewrite_type ends in `other => other` (589): any Expr/TypeExpr variant not explicitly enumerated is returned unchanged, with no qualification of embedded identifiers and no compile-time exhaustiveness error. Trigger: any fall-through variant carrying unqualified state/const/type names (including variants added later) yields unresolvable references in the lowered kernel; the catch-all makes the omission silent. Expr::Call likewise leaves its name unqualified (742-749), which is sound only if call names are always global.
finding.title: Non-exhaustive rewrite_expr/rewrite_type catch-alls (other => other) silently pass unhandled variants through without qualification
